title: IndigoZebra
summary: IndigoZebra is a espionage cluster that researchers have tracked since the mid 2010s, with activity reported against government, diplomatic, defence and telecommunications organisations in Central Asia and South Asia, and with lures frequently themed around regional political and security developments. The group's reported tradecraft centres on spear phishing that delivers a dropper, followed by a lightweight backdoor that provides file collection, command execution and screen or input monitoring capability, with command and control hosted on compromised legitimate websites rather than on attacker-registered infrastructure. Reporting has also described the use of cloud file sharing services for staging stolen documents, which means outbound traffic resembles normal business use. Attribution is not publicly settled: researchers have described overlaps with other Central Asia focused clusters and have used different names for related activity, so campaign ownership is often assessed on behaviour rather than on a single artefact. Evidence appears in mail gateway records, web server logs on the third-party site used for control, file creation and process execution telemetry on the victim host, and unusual outbound uploads. A common misunderstanding is that a compromised control server belongs to the attacker; in this pattern the attacker is a guest on someone else's site.

beginner.definition: IndigoZebra is a name researchers use for a group that spies on governments and telecom companies in Central and South Asia. Public reports describe it using fake messages to deliver harmful files. The name comes from security research, not from the group itself.
beginner.whyItMatters: This group hides its control traffic on real websites that it has broken into. That makes blocking harder, because the address looks legitimate. It also uploads stolen documents to ordinary file sharing services, so the theft looks like normal work. You need to look at patterns and volumes, not just at whether a destination is known to be bad.
howItWorks: The group writes an email about a topic the target follows, such as a regional security report.
The message carries a file or link that installs a small first-stage program.
That program contacts a website the group has already broken into.
The website hides the instructions, so the traffic looks like ordinary browsing.
The program then collects files, runs commands and can watch the screen.
Stolen documents are uploaded to normal file sharing services, which hides the theft.
beginner.example: Imagine a spy who never rents an office. Instead they hide messages in the classified ads of a local newspaper that everyone reads. The newspaper is legitimate and its address is trusted, so nobody blocks it. The spy simply reads the right page at the right time. Hiding control traffic on a compromised website works in exactly that way.
takeaways: Attackers can hide commands inside legitimate websites, so destination reputation is not enough.
Watch for unusual uploads to file sharing services, which can signal data theft.
Use behaviour and volume analysis when the destination looks trustworthy.

objectives: Explain how command and control hosted on compromised legitimate websites evades blocking.
Describe why uploads to cloud file sharing services can hide data exfiltration.
Identify host telemetry that reveals a dropper and its follow-on backdoor.
Explain how regional political themes are used to build convincing lures.
Describe how overlapping research clusters make campaign attribution uncertain.
